**Harold Holt and "All the way with LBJ"**
Holt was a Liberal prime minister who succeeded Robert Menzies in 1966 and backed the U.S. war in Vietnam, declaring that Australia would go "all the way with LBJ." In December 1967 he disappeared while swimming at Cheviot Beach in Victoria, and his body was never found.

**Robert Menzies and "The Forgotten People"**
Australia's longest-serving prime minister, who founded the modern Liberal Party and governed 1939–1941 and 1949–1966. His 1942 radio speech "The Forgotten People" praised the middle class as the backbone of the nation; his government handled the defection of Soviet spy Vladimir Petrov in 1954 and sent troops to the Malayan Emergency and Vietnam.

**Stolen Generations and Kevin Rudd's apology**
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, many of mixed descent, who were removed from their families by government policy and placed with white families or institutions, mostly from the late 19th century to the 1970s. The 1997 Bringing Them Home report documented the removals, National Sorry Day commemorates them, and Prime Minister Kevin Rudd issued a formal national apology in 2008 after John Howard had refused to.

**Rum Rebellion and William Bligh**
In 1808 officers of the New South Wales Corps led by George Johnston, encouraged by the wool pioneer John Macarthur, overthrew Governor William Bligh, who had earlier lost his ship in the Mutiny on the Bounty. The coup, named for the Corps' control of the rum trade, led Britain to appoint Lachlan Macquarie as governor.

**The Dismissal (1975)**
The constitutional crisis in which Governor-General Sir John Kerr removed Labor Prime Minister Gough Whitlam and appointed Liberal leader Malcolm Fraser as caretaker. It followed the Loans Affair, in which minister Rex Connor tried to raise overseas loans through the broker Tirath Khemlani, and the Senate's blocking of the budget; Whitlam is the only prime minister to be dismissed.

**Ned Kelly and the bushrangers**
Bushrangers were outlaws, often escaped convicts, who lived in the Australian bush. The most famous, Ned Kelly, killed three policemen at Stringybark Creek with his gang, including his brother Dan, and was captured in 1880 at Glenrowan wearing homemade iron armor before being hanged; Peter Carey's novel True History of the Kelly Gang fictionalizes his life.

**First Fleet, Arthur Phillip, and Botany Bay**
James Cook landed at Botany Bay on HMS Endeavour in 1770 and claimed eastern Australia for Britain. In 1788 Captain Arthur Phillip led the First Fleet of convict ships, settling at Port Jackson (Sydney) to found the penal colony of New South Wales.

**Eureka Stockade**
A 1854 rebellion by gold miners at Ballarat during the Victorian gold rush, protesting expensive mining licenses and lack of voting rights. Troops stormed the miners' stockade, but the revolt led to reforms and is seen as a founding moment of Australian democracy.

**White Australia policy**
The set of policies restricting non-European, especially Asian, immigration, formalized by the Immigration Restriction Act of 1901. It grew out of anti-Chinese violence during the gold rushes, such as the Buckland and Lambing Flat riots, and was dismantled in stages from the late 1940s to the 1970s.

**ANZAC and Gallipoli**
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps fought in the failed 1915 Gallipoli campaign against the Ottoman Empire in World War I. The landing is commemorated each year on ANZAC Day, April 25.

**John Curtin and the bombing of Darwin**
John Curtin was the Labor prime minister during most of World War II, when Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin in February 1942 and Japan fought Australians in the Territory of New Guinea. His successor Ben Chifley, who led postwar reconstruction, gave the "light on the hill" speech describing Labor's ideals.

**Mabo decision and terra nullius**
The 1992 High Court ruling in Mabo v. Queensland recognized native title for Indigenous Australians and rejected the doctrine of terra nullius, the claim that the land had belonged to no one before British settlement. Later that year Prime Minister Paul Keating acknowledged past injustices against Aboriginal people in his Redfern Speech.

**Black War in Van Diemen's Land**
The violent conflict between British settlers and Aboriginal Tasmanians (Palawa) in Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) in the 1820s and early 1830s. Governor George Arthur organized the "Black Line," a sweep by settlers to drive Aboriginal people from the settled districts, and George Augustus Robinson led "Friendly Missions" that relocated survivors.

**Burke and Wills expedition**
The 1860–1861 expedition sponsored by the Royal Society of Victoria to cross Australia from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria. Robert O'Hara Burke and William Wills reached the gulf but died on the return trip near Cooper Creek, where a "Dig Tree" marked buried supplies; John King was the only member of the final party to survive.

**Pacific Solution and the Tampa affair**
In 2001 the Norwegian freighter MV Tampa rescued 433 mostly Hazara asylum seekers, and John Howard's government refused to let them land in Australia. This led to the "Pacific Solution," under which asylum seekers were sent to offshore detention on Nauru and other places.
